prompt: Every change to the billing module takes three times longer because of tangled code. The team sets aside time each sprint to clean up the parts they touch most.
tells: clean up the parts they touch most
why: Fix debt where it costs you most.
trap: They may split work small, but the move is cleanup.

prompt: Instead of a two-year rewrite, the lead proposes improving the messy service piece by piece while still shipping features.
tells: improving the messy service piece by piece while still shipping features
why: Pay debt steadily, not in one risky rewrite.
trap: Piece by piece sounds like small changes, but the target is debt.

prompt: While adding a field, an engineer also renames a confusing function in the same file and adds a missing test, leaving it better than they found it.
tells: leaving it better than they found it
why: Small cleanups where you work keep debt down.
trap: It's a small, related cleanup, not an unrelated reformat.

prompt: Flaky tests make engineers rerun CI three times a day. The senior proposes a week to fix the worst ten.
tells: proposes a week to fix the worst ten
why: Target the debt that drags on everyone.
trap: Tests are involved, but the work is paying down a drag.

prompt: To win time for cleanup, a senior shows the product manager that half of last quarter's bugs came from one old module.
tells: half of last quarter's bugs came from one old module
why: Make the cost of debt visible to win time for it.
trap: Data is used, but to justify cleanup, not optimization.

prompt: In a behavioral interview, a candidate describes removing an old workaround that made every new screen take an extra day.
tells: removing an old workaround that made every new screen take an extra day
why: Remove shortcuts that keep costing time.
trap: The workaround wasn't speculative; it was a past shortcut.
